claim: Hydrogen peroxide is the most common reactive chemical that organisms face on the microbial battlefield.
source: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is the most common reactive chemical that organisms face on the microbial battlefield (Mishra and Imlay, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mishra and Imlay, 2012

claim: Bacteria, fungi, plants, and animal cells use H2O2 as an offensive weapon that damages nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids of their targets.
source: Bacteria, fungi, plants, and animal cells have long been known to use H2O2 as an offensive weapon that damages the nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids of their targets (Avery and Morgan, 1924; Imlay, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Avery and Morgan, 1924 and Imlay, 2018

claim: C. elegans encounter a wide variety of bacteria in their ecological setting.
source: C. elegans encounter a wide variety of bacteria in their ecological setting (Samuel et al., 2016; Schiffer et al., 2021), including many genera known to produce H2O2 (Passardi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Samuel et al., 2016 and Schiffer et al., 2021

claim: Many bacteria genera encountered by C. elegans are known to produce H2O2.
source: C. elegans encounter a wide variety of bacteria in their ecological setting (Samuel et al., 2016; Schiffer et al., 2021), including many genera known to produce H2O2 (Passardi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Passardi et al., 2007

claim: H2O2 produced by Neorhizobium sp. causes DNA damage to C. elegans nematodes.
source: H2O2 produced by a bacterium from the C. elegans microbiome, Neorhizobium sp., causes DNA damage to the nematodes (Kniazeva and Ruvkun, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kniazeva and Ruvkun, 2019

claim: Enterococcus faecium, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus oralis kill C. elegans by producing millimolar concentrations of hydrogen peroxide.
source: many bacteria—including Enterococcus faecium, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Streptococcus oralis—kill C. elegans by producing millimolar concentrations of hydrogen peroxide (Bolm et al., 2004; Jansen et al., 2002; Moy et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bolm et al., 2004; Jansen et al., 2002; Moy et al., 2004

claim: Prevention and repair of damage that hydrogen peroxide inflicts on macromolecules are critical for cellular health and survival.
source: Prevention and repair of the damage that hydrogen peroxide inflicts on macromolecules are critical for cellular health and survival (Chance et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chance et al., 1979

claim: C. elegans rely on conserved cellular defenses, including H2O2-degrading catalases, to avoid damage from H2O2.
source: To avoid damage from H2O2, C. elegans rely on conserved cellular defenses, including H2O2-degrading catalases (Chávez et al., 2007; Schiffer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chávez et al., 2007 and Schiffer et al., 2020

claim: Inducing H2O2 defenses at inappropriate times can cause undesirable side effects, including developmental defects.
source: However, inducing those defenses at inappropriate times can cause undesirable side effects, including developmental defects (Doonan et al., 2008; Kramer-Drauberg et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Doonan et al., 2008 and Kramer-Drauberg et al., 2020

claim: H2O2 modulates the function of proteins involved in signal transduction and differentiation.
source: because H2O2 modulates the function of proteins involved in a wide variety of cellular processes, including signal transduction and differentiation (Hourihan et al., 2016; Kramer-Drauberg et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021; Veal et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hourihan et al., 2016; Kramer-Drauberg et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021; Veal et al., 2007

claim: 10 classes of sensory neurons in the brain of C. elegans manage the challenge of deciding when the nematode's tissues induce H2O2 defenses.
source: We recently found that 10 classes of sensory neurons in the brain of C. elegans manage the challenge of deciding when the nematode's tissues induce H2O2 defenses (Schiffer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schiffer et al., 2020

claim: Temperature affects the growth of bacteria.
source: Temperature also affects the growth of bacteria (Barber, 1908; Rosso et al., 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barber, 1908 and Rosso et al., 1993

claim: Temperature likely affects the interactions of C. elegans with beneficial and pathogenic bacteria.
source: and, therefore, likely affects the interactions of C. elegans with beneficial and pathogenic bacteria (Samuel et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Samuel et al., 2016 and Zhang et al., 2017

claim: C. elegans adjust their behavior and physiology in response to the perception of temperature by sensory neurons.
source: While nematodes do not regulate their own body temperature, they adjust their behavior and physiology in response to the perception of temperature by sensory neurons, enabling them to seek temperatures conducive to survival, avoid noxious temperature ranges, and induce heat defenses (Goodman and Sengupta, 2019; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Prahlad et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodman and Sengupta, 2019; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Prahlad et al., 2008

claim: Nematodes perceive temperature via seven classes of sensory neurons.
source: Nematodes perceive temperature, in part, via seven classes of sensory neurons (Beverly et al., 2011; Biron et al., 2008; Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Kuhara et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Mori and Ohshima, 1995; Schild et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beverly et al., 2011; Biron et al., 2008; Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Kuhara et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Mori and Ohshima, 1995; Schild et al., 2014

claim: Four classes of temperature-sensing neurons regulate C. elegans peroxide resistance.
source: Previously, we found that four of those classes of neurons regulate C. elegans peroxide resistance (Schiffer et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schiffer et al., 2020

claim: The lethality of hydrogen peroxide to C. elegans increases with temperature.
source: Here, we show that the lethality of hydrogen peroxide to C. elegans increases with temperature.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2A, 2B)

claim: Nematodes partially compensate for increased H2O2 lethality at high temperature by preemptively inducing their hydrogen peroxide defenses.
source: Nematodes partially compensate for this by preemptively inducing their hydrogen peroxide defenses at high temperature.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2C, 2D)

claim: The temperature-dependent regulation of peroxide defenses enables nematodes to better cope with H2O2 produced by the pathogenic bacterium E. faecium.
source: This adaptive response to temperature enables the nematodes to better cope with H2O2 produced by the pathogenic bacterium E. faecium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2E)

claim: The temperature-dependent regulation of peroxide defenses is directed by the AFD sensory neurons.
source: The temperature-dependent regulation of peroxide defenses is directed by the AFD sensory neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3D, 3E)

claim: At high temperature, the AFD neurons repress the expression of the INS-39 insulin/IGF1 hormone.
source: At high temperature, the AFD neurons repress the expression of the INS-39 insulin/IGF1 hormone
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5C, 5D)

claim: Repression of INS-39 expression alleviates inhibition by insulin/IGF1 signaling of the nematodes' peroxide defenses.
source: and thereby alleviate inhibition by insulin/IGF1 signaling of the nematodes' peroxide defenses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from genetic experiments (Figure 5F, 5G)

claim: The insulin/IGF1 effector DAF-16/FOXO functions in intestinal cells to determine the size of gene-expression changes induced by the absence of signals from the AFD neurons.
source: The insulin/IGF1 effector DAF-16/FOXO functions in intestinal cells to determine the size of the gene-expression changes induced by the absence of signals from the AFD neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tissue-specific rescue experiments and transcriptomic analysis (Figure 6E, 6F, Figure 8G)

claim: This is the first example of a multicellular organism inducing their defenses to a chemical when they sense an inherent enhancer of the reactivity of that chemical.
source: This is the first example of a multicellular organism inducing their defenses to a chemical when they sense an inherent enhancer of the reactivity of that chemical.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: Chemical reactions occur at faster rates at higher temperatures.
source: That threat is inherently temperature dependent because chemical reactions occur at faster rates at higher temperatures (Arrhenius, 1889; Evans and Polanyi, 1935; Eyring, 1935).
evidence: Supported by citations to fundamental chemical kinetics principles (Arrhenius, 1889; Evans and Polanyi, 1935; Eyring, 1935)

claim: The Fenton reaction of H2O2 with DNA-bound Fe(II) is predicted to be 40% faster at 25°C than at 20°C.
source: The Fenton reaction of H2O2 with DNA-bound Fe(II), which leads to DNA damage, was predicted to be 40% faster at 25°C than at 20°C (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on chemical kinetics modeling shown in Figure 1

claim: Oxidation of thiol groups of cysteines by H2O2 is predicted to be more than twofold faster for regular cysteines in proteins at 25°C compared to 20°C.
source: For the oxidation of the thiol groups of cysteines, reaction rates with H2O2 were predicted to be more than twofold faster for regular cysteines in proteins, 62% faster for free cysteines, up to 56% faster for very reactive cysteines such as the redox-sensitive cysteine residue of GAPDH, and 17% faster for the most reactive cysteines of hydroperoxidases (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on chemical kinetics modeling shown in Figure 1

claim: Oxidation of free cysteines by H2O2 is predicted to be 62% faster at 25°C compared to 20°C.
source: For the oxidation of the thiol groups of cysteines, reaction rates with H2O2 were predicted to be more than twofold faster for regular cysteines in proteins, 62% faster for free cysteines, up to 56% faster for very reactive cysteines such as the redox-sensitive cysteine residue of GAPDH, and 17% faster for the most reactive cysteines of hydroperoxidases (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on chemical kinetics modeling shown in Figure 1

claim: Oxidation of very reactive cysteines such as the redox-sensitive cysteine residue of GAPDH by H2O2 is predicted to be up to 56% faster at 25°C compared to 20°C.
source: For the oxidation of the thiol groups of cysteines, reaction rates with H2O2 were predicted to be more than twofold faster for regular cysteines in proteins, 62% faster for free cysteines, up to 56% faster for very reactive cysteines such as the redox-sensitive cysteine residue of GAPDH, and 17% faster for the most reactive cysteines of hydroperoxidases (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on chemical kinetics modeling shown in Figure 1

claim: Oxidation of the most reactive cysteines of hydroperoxidases by H2O2 is predicted to be 17% faster at 25°C compared to 20°C.
source: For the oxidation of the thiol groups of cysteines, reaction rates with H2O2 were predicted to be more than twofold faster for regular cysteines in proteins, 62% faster for free cysteines, up to 56% faster for very reactive cysteines such as the redox-sensitive cysteine residue of GAPDH, and 17% faster for the most reactive cysteines of hydroperoxidases (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on chemical kinetics modeling shown in Figure 1

claim: When tBuOOH concentration exceeded 0.75 mM, C. elegans lifespan was shortened by 50% by each additional 45% increase in tBuOOH concentration.
source: Previously, we found that when tBuOOH concentration exceeded 0.75 mM, C. elegans lifespan was shortened by 50% by each additional 45% increase in tBuOOH concentration (Stroustrup et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stroustrup et al., 2016

claim: In the presence of 6 mM tBuOOH, nematodes grown at 20°C survived an average of 1.6 days at 20°C.
source: In the presence of 6 mM tBuOOH, nematodes grown at 20°C survived an average of 1.6 days at 20°C, while those grown and assayed at 25°C survived 30% shorter (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Nematodes grown and assayed at 25°C survived 30% shorter in 6 mM tBuOOH compared to those grown and assayed at 20°C.
source: In the presence of 6 mM tBuOOH, nematodes grown at 20°C survived an average of 1.6 days at 20°C, while those grown and assayed at 25°C survived 30% shorter (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Nematodes grown and assayed at 25°C were less likely to survive E. faecium supernatant compared to those grown and assayed at 20°C.
source: Compared to nematodes grown and assayed at 20°C, those grown and assayed at 25°C were less likely to survive the E. faecium supernatant (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: In survival assays performed at 25°C, nematodes grown at 25°C lived 54% longer than those grown at 20°C.
source: To our surprise, we found that in survival assays performed at 25°C the nematodes grown at 25°C lived 54% longer than those grown at 20°C (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In assays performed at 20°C, nematodes grown at 25°C lived 57% longer than those grown at 20°C.
source: Similarly, in assays performed at 20°C, the nematodes grown at 25°C lived 57% longer than those grown at 20°C (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: A higher proportion of nematodes grown at 25°C survived exposure to E. faecium liquid-culture supernatant at 20°C compared to nematodes grown at 20°C.
source: We also found that, compared with nematodes grown at 20°C, a higher proportion of nematodes grown at 25°C survived exposure to E. faecium liquid-culture supernatant at 20°C (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Shifting from 20 to 25°C for 2 days was sufficient to improve peroxide survival at 25°C.
source: Shifting from 20 to 25°C for 2 days was sufficient to improve peroxide survival at 25°C, but shifting only 1 day before the assay was not sufficient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Shifting from 20 to 25°C only 1 day before the assay was not sufficient to improve peroxide survival at 25°C.
source: Shifting from 20 to 25°C for 2 days was sufficient to improve peroxide survival at 25°C, but shifting only 1 day before the assay was not sufficient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Nematodes down-shifted from 25 to 20°C for 2 days, 1 day, or immediately before the assay were all more peroxide resistant at 20°C than those grown continuously at 20°C.
source: Nematodes down-shifted from 25 to 20°C for 2 days, 1 day, or immediately before the assay were all more peroxide resistant at 20°C than those grown continuously at 20°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Growth at 25°C can increase the nematodes' peroxide resistance even days after they have been transferred to 20°C.
source: Therefore, growth at 25°C could increase the nematodes' peroxide resistance even days after they had been transferred to 20°C.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: When grown at 20°C, tax-4 mutants exhibited an over twofold increase in peroxide resistance at 20°C relative to wild-type controls.
source: When grown at 20°C, tax-4 mutants exhibited an over twofold increase in peroxide resistance at 20°C relative to wild-type controls (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: When grown and assayed at 25°C, tax-4 mutants exhibited a 49% increase in peroxide resistance.
source: In contrast, when grown and assayed at 25°C, tax-4 mutants exhibited a smaller increase in peroxide resistance, 49% (Figure 3C).

claim: Compared with wild-type nematodes, when grown and assayed at 20°C, AFD-ablated nematodes exhibited an over twofold increase in resistance to tBuOOH.
source: Compared with wild-type nematodes, when grown and assayed at 20°C, the AFD-ablated nematodes exhibited an over twofold increase in resistance to tBuOOH (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: AFD-ablated nematodes exhibited an over twofold increase in resistance to H2O2 at 20°C compared to wild-type nematodes.
source: and H2O2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)

claim: AFD-ablated nematodes were more likely to survive exposure to E. faecium liquid-culture supernatant at 20°C compared to wild-type nematodes.
source: and were more likely to survive exposure to E. faecium liquid-culture supernatant (Figure 3F).

claim: At 25°C, AFD ablation increased resistance to tBuOOH by 31%.
source: At 25°C, AFD ablation increased resistance to tBuOOH by 31% (Figure 3E), a much smaller amount than at 20°C.

claim: AFD-ablated nematodes grown at 25°C exhibited the same levels of peroxide resistance as wild-type nematodes grown at 25°C.
source: Consistent with that prediction, AFD-ablated nematodes grown at 25°C exhibited the same levels of resistance as wild-type nematodes grown at 25°C (Figure 3G, H).

claim: AFD-ablated nematodes grown continuously at 20°C exhibited the highest levels of peroxide resistance.
source: AFD-ablated nematodes grown continuously at 20°C exhibited the highest levels of peroxide resistance (Figure 3H).

claim: At 20°C, the gcy-8(oy44), gcy-18(nj38), and gcy-23(oy150) single mutants increased peroxide resistance by 10%, 51%, and 21%, respectively, relative to wild-type controls.
source: At 20°C, the gcy-8(oy44), gcy-18(nj38), and gcy-23(oy150) single mutants increased peroxide resistance by 10%, 51%, and 21%, respectively, relative to wild-type controls (Figure 3L).

claim: Relative to nematodes grown at 20°C, those grown at 25°C had lower expression of 2446 genes and higher expression of 809 genes, out of 18039 genes detected (q value <0.01).
source: Relative to nematodes grown at 20°C, those grown at 25°C had lower expression of 2446 genes and higher expression of 809 genes, out of 18039 genes detected (q value <0.01) (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: AFD ablation lowered the expression of 2077 genes and increased the expression of 2225 genes, out of 7912 genes detected (q value <0.01).
source: AFD ablation lowered the expression of 2077 genes and increased the expression of 2225 genes, out of 7912 genes detected (q value <0.01) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by mRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Higher cultivation temperature and ablation of the AFD neurons induced changes in gene expression that were linearly correlated in a positive manner (R2 = 9%, p < 0.0001).
source: We found that both interventions induced changes in gene expression that were linearly correlated in a positive manner (R2 = 9%, p < 0.0001, Figure 4C).

claim: Genes with either higher or lower expression in both wild-type nematodes at 25°C and AFD-ablated nematodes at 20°C were disproportionally enriched.

claim: Both higher temperature and AFD ablation downregulated genes associated with reproduction and with expression in the germline.

claim: Both higher temperature and AFD ablation upregulated genes associated with defense and immune responses and with expression in the intestine.

claim: Higher temperature and AFD ablation induced positively correlated changes in the average expression of gene sets affecting similar biological processes (R2 = 24%, p < 0.0001).

claim: Both growth at 25°C and ablation of AFD at 20°C increased the expression of genes induced when nematodes were exposed to tert-butyl hydroperoxide.

claim: Wild-type nematodes grown at 25°C had 73% higher levels of ctl-2 expression compared to nematodes grown at 20°C.

claim: Ablation of the AFD neurons increased ctl-1 expression by 46%.

claim: The daf-16(mu86) null mutation caused a 21% reduction in peroxide resistance in nematodes grown and assayed at 20°C.
